## CIEC-9(b)

### Question

Has Mr. Velez analyzed the level of heat pump adoption at which the Company’s distribution system, or individual substations or feeders, would become winter peaking? If so, provide the analysis. If not, explain why not.

### Response

No. I have not analyzed the level of heat pump adoption at which the Company’s distribution system as a whole, or any individual substation or feeder, would become winter peaking. I did not run heat pump adoption scenarios against the system peak or against any substation or feeder, and I do not have an estimate of that adoption level for any of them.

**What the record shows about the peak today.** The record describes the season of the peak in recent years and in the Company’s forecast. It does not show at what level of heat pump adoption that would change.

- The Company’s sales forecast adds heat pump energy in October through April and does not add heat pump load to the peak forecast, “since the peak occurs in July and there are no heating loads at that time” (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-002 at 1) [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].
- The Company “does not use a heat pump forecast to inform its substation capacity projects as the system remains summer peaking” (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-020 at 1) [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].
- The Company’s marginal cost study derives a probability of peak from 2022 through 2025 hourly distribution substation load. About 80 percent of the annual probability of peak falls in July and August, 19.5 percent in June and September, and less than 1 percent in December and January (Nieto Direct, Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1, at 12:5–13 and 18:7–10) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026d]. The testimony states that the analysis accounts for heat pump adoption through 2031 (_id._ at 6:9–12, 12:11–13). The steps described in the Company’s response to OCC-733, and the data in OCC-733 Attachment 1, show an adjustment for behind-the-meter solar only [@clp_Docket260510OCC733_2026].
- The same testimony states that “[o]nly a very small number of bulk substations experience a peak load in the winter months of December or January,” and that those substations have higher load-carrying capability in winter than in summer (Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1 at 18:10–13) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026d]. It does not identify those substations or give their loads.

**The distribution system as a whole.** For the system as a whole, the record contains the main input such an analysis would start from: the Company’s hourly load summed across all of its distribution substations, January 2022 through December 2025, produced as OCC-733 Attachment 1 [@clp_Docket260510OCC733_2026]. With an estimate of the winter peak demand each heat pump home adds, which my testimony develops from ResStock, and a forecast of adoption, that series would support an estimate of the adoption level at which the system’s winter peak would exceed its summer peak. ISO New England publishes a heat pump adoption forecast and its contribution to the winter peak for the Connecticut load zone, which also includes customers of other utilities [@isone_Final2026Heat_2026]. The Company’s own heat pump forecasts have not been released (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-021 at 1) [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c]. I did not make that estimate. **[TK: JPV: state the reason. A candidate, if it is accurate: the Company adds distribution capacity substation by substation and feeder by feeder, against each one’s own peak and rating, so the date at which the system sum turns winter peaking would not by itself show when, or whether, heat pump load requires new distribution capacity.]**

**Substations and feeders.** For each substation and feeder, the analysis would require three things: its current summer and winter peak loads, its summer and winter ratings, and the number of heat pump customers it serves, or a forecast of how many it will serve, so that their added winter demand can be assigned to it. The Company has not provided the first two, and it says it does not have the third. The data it has produced does not substitute for them.

System Data Requirement No. 2, produced as OCC-365, Attachment 28, on September 1, 2026, gives for each distribution circuit one capacity, in kVA, the annual maximum and minimum loading for 2021 through 2025, and a customer count. It does not give the date or season of the maximum, a winter peak, a winter rating, a forecast, or a count of heat pump customers. That table supports Figure 11 of my direct testimony: of the 918 feeders with loading data, the median feeder peaks at 49 percent of its rating, and 2 exceed their rating [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026, p. 21, lines 5–8]. Because the season of each peak is not identified, the table cannot show whether any feeder peaks in winter today, or how much winter load it could add before it did [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026, p. 22, lines 1–2]. The Company also states that no substation transformer is loaded above 100 percent of nameplate under normal conditions (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-018 at 2) [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]. That statement does not give a seasonal peak or rating either.

The following information would be needed for the substation and feeder analysis. None of it is in the public record of this docket.

| Information needed | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Summer and winter peak load, with date and hour, for each feeder and substation transformer, 2023–2025 | Requested in CLF-SC-013(a) and CLF-SC-017(a). Withheld as Critical Energy Infrastructure Information pending a non-disclosure agreement. Not received. |
| Summer and winter normal ratings for each feeder and substation transformer | Requested in CLF-SC-012 and CLF-SC-016. Withheld on the same basis. Not received. |
| Hourly metered load for each feeder and substation transformer | Requested in CLF-SC-015 and CLF-SC-019. Withheld on the same basis. Not received. |
| Heat pump customers served by each feeder or substation transformer | Requested in CLF-SC-012(h) and CLF-SC-016(h). The Company says it has no comprehensive list of customers who heat with heat pumps, and does not track customer counts at the bulk transformer level. |
| Forecast summer and winter peaks for each feeder and substation transformer | Requested in CLF-SC-013(b) and CLF-SC-017(b). The Company says it does not produce feeder-level or transformer-level forecasts. |
| A winter peak forecast, and the heat pump contribution to forecast peak demand | Requested in CLF-SC-001(c), CLF-SC-020 and CLF-SC-021. The Company applies no heat pump adjustment to forecast peak demand. Its winter peak forecast is incomplete and unreleased, reaches only a preliminary substation level, and is to include feeders and transformers in the 2028 forecast. Its heat pump forecasts have not been released. |
| Hourly load of customers with heat pumps | Requested in CLF-SC-008. The Company says it does not employ AMI meters and does not have the data. |

The withheld items are addressed in CL&P Responses to CLF-SC-012 at 1–2, CLF-SC-013(a) at 2, CLF-SC-015 at 2, CLF-SC-016 at 1–2, CLF-SC-017(a) at 2, and CLF-SC-019 at 2 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]. The Company’s statements about what it does not have are in CL&P Responses to CLF-SC-001(c) at 2, CLF-SC-008 at 1, CLF-SC-012 at 2, CLF-SC-013(b) at 2, CLF-SC-016 at 2, CLF-SC-017(b) at 2, and CLF-SC-020 at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b], and CLF-SC-021 at 1 and CLF-SC-022 at 2 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c].

I also have not found this information in the Company’s public filings outside this docket. The Company’s public hosting capacity map gives one rating for each circuit, in amps, and for each substation, in MVA, and its electric vehicle hosting capacity map gives an amount of new load each feeder can take. Neither gives peak loads or seasonal ratings.^[Eversource, Connecticut Hosting Capacity Map, DG and EV hosting capacity layers, updated November 21, 2025 **[NOT INGESTED]**.] The Company’s 2026 Forecast of Loads and Resources reports its annual summer peak for 2021 through 2025 and forecasts it through 2035. It reports no winter peak. It states that heat pumps are “expected to convert a large portion of the system to winter peaking in 1 to 2 decades,” and that its adoption model is “aggregated by substation,” but it gives no substation or feeder results.^[Eversource Energy, 2026 Forecast of Loads and Resources, filed with the Connecticut Siting Council April 1, 2026, Table 2-1 and § 2.4 **[NOT INGESTED]**.]

I will supplement this response if the Company produces the seasonal peaks, ratings, and hourly loads.

## Record check

This section is a working note. It is not part of the response.

**What the response does not claim.** It does not say that the system will or will not become winter peaking, or when, and it does not say that feeders or substations would become winter peaking first. No analysis we performed or found supports any of those statements. It does not say that the system-level data were unavailable: they are public, in OCC-733 Attachment 1. It does not say that the withheld substation and feeder data do not exist: the Company has them and withheld them pending a non-disclosure agreement, which has not led to a production.

**System-level data that is available, and what we did with it.**

- **OCC-733 Attachment 1** (filed September 28, 2026; PDF, 413 pages, and Excel). Hourly series, January 1, 2022 through December 31, 2025, 35,064 rows. Columns: DateTime, Year, Month, Day, Hour, Weekday, Total, Lost load PV, Net Load. Units are not labeled; the magnitudes are consistent with MW. “Lost load PV” is the Company’s projected behind-the-meter solar addition (the sheet notes a source of “PV additions through 2032”), so Net Load is a projection, not a metered load. There is no heat pump column. Read from the PDF on PURA on November 14, 2026; not ingested. **[TK: Alex Lee: download the Excel version from the filing page (OCC-731 to 741, filed 09/28/2026) and ingest it.]**
- Seasonal maxima read from that attachment (June–September versus December–February):

  | Year | Summer max, Total | Winter max, Total | Summer max, Net | Winter max, Net |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 2022 | 4,525 (Aug 9) | 3,198 (Jan 11) | 4,139 (Jul 20) | 3,198 (Jan 11) |
  | 2023 | 4,367 (Jul 6) | 3,220 (Feb 4) | 4,077 (Sep 7) | 3,201 (Feb 3) |
  | 2024 | 4,467 (Jul 16) | 3,176 (Jan 17) | 4,041 (Jul 16) | 3,070 (Dec 23) |
  | 2025 | 4,638 (Jul 29) | 3,428 (Jan 22) | 4,220 (Jul 29) | 3,203 (Jan 22) |

  These are not in the response. They are consistent with the record statements that the system is summer peaking today. They do not tell us the adoption level at which that would change.
- **ISO-NE 2026 heat pump forecast** (ingested as `isone_Final2026Heat_2026`): Connecticut zone heat pump contribution to the winter 50/50 peak, 35 MW in 2026 rising to 874 MW in 2035. The Connecticut zone includes UI and municipal utilities.
- **ISO-NE 2026 CELT:** regional and zonal summer and winter 50/50 and 90/10 net peaks. Regionally, the 90/10 winter peak exceeds the 50/50 summer peak by 2034, and winter becomes the prevailing peak season in the late 2030s. Zonal values are in the CELT forecast data workbook. Not ingested.
- **Eversource 2026 Forecast of Loads and Resources** (Connecticut Siting Council): CL&P summer peak, actual 2021–2025 (5,078 MW in 2025) and forecast through 2035. No winter peak.
- **What we did:** our only use of system-level hourly load was ISO-NE regional load for the bulk transmission probability of peak (Exhibit JPV-2, Section 3). No winter-versus-summer crossover analysis was performed at any level.

**Where the response’s facts come from.**

| Statement | Source | What it does and does not show |

| Probability of peak by month; testimony says heat pump adoption through 2031 is included | Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1 at 6:9–12, 12:5–13, 18:7–10 | The Company’s shape through 2031. Gives no adoption level at which winter overtakes summer. |
| Probability-of-peak steps and data show a solar adjustment only | OCC-733 at 1–2 and Attachment 1 | No heat pump step is described and the data have no heat pump column. |
| A very small number of bulk substations peak in December or January | Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1 at 18:10–13 | Current state. Substations not identified; no loads given. |
| Hourly load summed across all distribution substations, 2022–2025 | OCC-733 Attachment 1 | System level only. No substation or feeder detail. |
| 918 feeders, median at 49 percent of rating, 2 above rating | OCC-365, Attachment 28; Velez Direct at 21:5–8 | Annual maximum only. Season unknown. |

**Checked on November 14, 2026.**

- The ingested CLF-SC responses, CLF-SC-001 through CLF-SC-035, and Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1.
- The Docket 26-05-10 index on the PURA site. Under “Interrogs from Sierra Club to CL&P 1 thru 20,” the only responses are the September 18, 2026 filings; none is a supplement.
- OCC-365, Attachment 28, on its September 1, 2026 filing page. Its columns are substation, circuit, capacity, annual maximum and minimum loading for 2021 through 2025, customer count, and a demand-to-capacity ratio.
- OCC-733 and its Attachment 1, on the September 28, 2026 filing page for OCC-731 to OCC-741.
- Docket filing titles. None describes a feeder or substation seasonal-peak production. The protective-order motions whose titles do not name a set (Motions 035, 039, 110, 114, 115, and 116) cover OCC, EOE, and PURA sets.
- Eversource’s public hosting capacity services for Connecticut (ArcGIS REST, `dghostingexternalmapprod.eversource.com`): the DG hosting layer has `CIRCUIT_RATING_AMPS`, `DIST_SUB_RATING_MVA`, `BULK_SUB_RATING_MVA` and hosting capacity in MW, updated November 21, 2025. The EV hosting layer has `FEEDER_CAPACITY_TO_MAP_MW` by circuit and substation. The other public folders are reliability circuits and substation locations. No layer has peak load, season of peak, or seasonal ratings. Eversource’s new parcel-based map is described as showing “seasonal and time-series hosting capacity, along with available headroom” for a selected parcel. It is an interactive tool, not a dataset, and was not checked parcel by parcel.
- Eversource 2026 and 2025 Forecasts of Loads and Resources (Connecticut Siting Council). Summer peaks only. The 2026 Forecast states that heat pumps are expected to make “a large portion of the system” winter peaking “in 1 to 2 decades,” with no numbers by substation.
- ISO-NE 2026 CELT final draft load forecast slides (March 27, 2026) and CELT public webinar (June 24, 2026).
- PURA Grid Modernization page (Docket 17-12-03 and its reopeners). None is a distribution plan filing with substation or feeder seasonal loads. The non-wires solutions process (17-12-03RE07; first cycle in Docket 25-08-08) has Eversource file grid needs, with distribution needs data shared under non-disclosure and CEII agreements; the 2025 cycle identified one Eversource project, the West Brookfield substation transformer replacement. The Docket 25-08-08 filings themselves were not opened.
- DEEP Conservation and Load Management technical meeting minutes (November 21, 2024): the utilities said they had not investigated a shift to winter peaking as part of active demand response.
